content.text:
I submitted **part-based** with confidence 0.75. The evidence leans that way but isn't conclusive, because the test results were very noisy.

**Design:** I trained the learner on three tasks that between them use three of the four rules in each dimension: L1-S1-M1, L2-S2-M2 and L3-S3-M3. I then tested other tasks grouped by how many of their rules the learner had never seen. I repeated tests across many tasks because the same task could score anywhere from 1 to 41 examples.

**Results** (average examples needed to reach criterion):

| Rules new to the learner | Mean | Number of tests |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | 17.6 | 22 |
| 1 | 23.9 | 22 |
| 2 | 41.7 | 3 |
| 3 (L4-S4-M4) | 37.6 | 8 |

**Why part-based:**
- **Cost tracks new rules.** It rises with the number of new rules. The 2-new group is a bit above the 3-new group, but it has only 3 tests.
- **The deciding comparison goes against holistic.** Every 1-new task I tested (such as L1-S4-M1) shares two rules with one trained task, so it looks more similar to it as a whole. Some 0-new tasks, such as L1-S2-M3, share at most one rule with any trained task. A holistic learner measuring similarity like this should find the 1-new tasks easier, but they came out harder.
- **Output overlap didn't predict anything.** How often a test task gives the same response as a trained task (`compare`) did not predict its cost. L4-S2-M2 has 0% overlap with any trained task, and one of its tests took just 1 example.

**Caveats:**
- Roughly one standard error separates the 0-new and 1-new averages, so that difference is suggestive rather than decisive. The gap between known-rule tasks and the 2- and 3-new tasks is much clearer.
- The holistic learner's similarity measure is hidden. It could happen to follow rule novelty, which would make the two hypotheses look the same here.

I used all 60 of the budget, including two tests before training.
